summary.text: For the candidate linear-recurrence sequence \(c_n\), the defect \(d_n=c_{n+1}^2-c_nc_{n+2}\) satisfies \(d_{n+3}=4d_{n+1}+d_n\); simultaneous induction with the growth of \(c_n\) proves \(0<d_n\le c_n\). Hence \(c_{n+1}^2=c_nc_{n+2}+d_n\) makes \(\lceil c_{n+1}^2/c_n\rceil-1=c_{n+2}\), so induction identifies the originally defined terms with the linear-recurrence sequence and yields its generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) denote the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer whose ratio to \(b_{n+1}\) is strictly smaller than \(b_{n+1}/b_n\). Once positivity is known, this says
\[
b_{n+2}=\left\lceil \frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the ratio inequality is equivalent to
\[
b_{n+2}<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n},
\]
and for any real number \(x\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(x\) is \(\lceil x\rceil-1\). We will prove positivity along the way by identifying \(b_n\) with an explicitly positive sequence.

We shall prove that
\[
b_0=4,\quad b_1=16,\quad b_2=63,
\]
and, for all \(n\ge 3\),
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}. \tag{2}
\]
This recurrence is equivalent to the claimed generating function.

Define an integer sequence \((c_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
c_0=4,\qquad c_1=16,\qquad c_2=63,
\]
and
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n \qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{3}
\]
The first few values are
\[
c_0=4,\quad c_1=16,\quad c_2=63,\quad c_3=248,\quad c_4=976.
\]
The main task is to show that the rounding rule (1) produces exactly this sequence.

We first establish a useful positivity and growth estimate:
\[
0<c_n\quad\text{and}\quad 3c_n\le c_{n+1}\qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{4}
\]
We prove these two assertions simultaneously by strong induction. For \(n=0,1,2\), they follow directly from
\[
(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3)=(4,16,63,248):
\]
we have \(12\le16\), \(48\le63\), and \(189\le248\), and all four displayed terms are positive.

Now suppose the assertions are known at all indices below \(k+3\). By (3),
\[
c_{k+3}=4c_{k+2}-c_k.
\]
The induction hypotheses give \(c_{k+2}\ge 3c_{k+1}\ge 9c_k\), with \(c_k>0\). In particular \(4c_{k+2}-c_k>0\), so \(c_{k+3}>0\). For the growth estimate at index \(k+3\), use (3) once more:
\[
c_{k+4}-3c_{k+3}
=(4c_{k+3}-c_{k+1})-3c_{k+3}
=c_{k+3}-c_{k+1}.
\]
But \(c_{k+3}\ge 3c_{k+2}\ge c_{k+1}\), so this difference is nonnegative. Hence \(3c_{k+3}\le c_{k+4}\). This proves (4).

The quantity that controls the rounding in (1) is the difference between \(c_{n+1}^2\) and \(c_nc_{n+2}\). Introduce an auxiliary integer sequence \((d_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
d_0=4,\qquad d_1=1,\qquad d_2=16,
\]
and
\[
d_{n+3}=4d_{n+1}+d_n \qquad(n\ge0). \tag{5}
\]
We need two facts about this sequence:
\[
0<d_n\le c_n \qquad(n\ge0), \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
c_{n+1}^2=c_nc_{n+2}+d_n \qquad(n\ge0). \tag{7}
\]

We prove (6) first, again by strong induction. At the initial indices,
\[
(d_0,d_1,d_2)=(4,1,16),\qquad (c_0,c_1,c_2)=(4,16,63),
\]
so the assertion is immediate.

For the induction step, suppose the bounds hold at the earlier relevant indices. From (5),
\[
d_{k+3}=4d_{k+1}+d_k,
\]
which is positive because \(d_{k+1}\) and \(d_k\) are positive. Also, using the induction hypotheses,
\[
d_{k+3}\le 4c_{k+1}+c_k. \tag{8}
\]
We claim that the right-hand side is at most \(c_{k+3}\). By (3), it suffices to show
\[
4c_{k+1}+c_k\le 4c_{k+2}-c_k,
\]
or equivalently
\[
4c_{k+1}+2c_k\le 4c_{k+2}. \tag{9}
\]
The growth estimates (4) give \(c_{k+2}\ge3c_{k+1}\) and \(c_{k+1}\ge3c_k\). Thus
\[
4c_{k+2}\ge12c_{k+1}\ge4c_{k+1}+2c_k,
\]
which proves (9). Combining this with (8) gives \(d_{k+3}\le c_{k+3}\), completing the proof of (6).

We next prove the key identity (7). Let
\[
e_n:=c_{n+1}^2-c_nc_{n+2}.
\]
A direct calculation of the first three values gives
\[
e_0=16^2-4\cdot63=256-252=4,
\]
\[
e_1=63^2-16\cdot248=3969-3968=1,
\]
and, since \(c_4=4\cdot248-16=976\),
\[
e_2=248^2-63\cdot976=61504-61488=16.
\]
Thus \((e_0,e_1,e_2)=(4,1,16)=(d_0,d_1,d_2)\).

We now show that \(e_n\) satisfies the same recurrence as \(d_n\). Fix \(k\), and abbreviate
\[
u=c_{k+3}=4c_{k+2}-c_k,
\]
\[
v=c_{k+4}=4u-c_{k+1},
\]
\[
w=c_{k+5}=4v-c_{k+2}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{k+3}
&=c_{k+4}^2-c_{k+3}c_{k+5}\\
&=v^2-u(4v-c_{k+2})\\
&=v(v-4u)+uc_{k+2}\\
&=-c_{k+1}v+uc_{k+2}\\
&=-c_{k+1}(4u-c_{k+1})+uc_{k+2}\\
&=c_{k+1}^2+u(c_{k+2}-4c_{k+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting \(u=4c_{k+2}-c_k\) and expanding gives
\[
e_{k+3}
=4c_{k+2}^2-16c_{k+1}c_{k+2}+4c_kc_{k+1}
+c_{k+1}^2-c_kc_{k+2}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
4e_{k+1}+e_k
&=4\bigl(c_{k+2}^2-c_{k+1}c_{k+3}\bigr)
 +\bigl(c_{k+1}^2-c_kc_{k+2}\bigr)\\
&=4c_{k+2}^2-4c_{k+1}(4c_{k+2}-c_k)
 +c_{k+1}^2-c_kc_{k+2},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is exactly the same expression. Therefore
\[
e_{k+3}=4e_{k+1}+e_k. \tag{10}
\]
The initial values of \(e_n\) equal those of \(d_n\), and (10) is the recurrence (5). Strong induction therefore yields \(e_n=d_n\) for every \(n\), which is precisely (7).

Combining (6) and (7), we obtain for every \(n\)
\[
c_{n+1}^2=c_nc_{n+2}+d_n,
\qquad 1\le d_n\le c_n. \tag{11}
\]
Here the lower bound \(1\le d_n\) follows because \(d_n\) is a positive integer. Consequently,
\[
\frac{c_{n+1}^2}{c_n}=c_{n+2}+\frac{d_n}{c_n},
\qquad 0<\frac{d_n}{c_n}\le1.
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
\left\lceil\frac{c_{n+1}^2}{c_n}\right\rceil=c_{n+2}+1,
\]
and hence
\[
\left\lceil\frac{c_{n+1}^2}{c_n}\right\rceil-1=c_{n+2}. \tag{12}
\]
Notice that (12) includes both possibilities: if \(d_n<c_n\), the fractional part is strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), while if \(d_n=c_n\), the quotient is exactly \(c_{n+2}+1\). In either case its ceiling is \(c_{n+2}+1\).

Equivalently, if the ceiling is written using integer division, (11) gives
\[
c_{n+1}^2+c_n-1=c_nc_{n+2}+(d_n+c_n-1).
\]
Since \(1\le d_n\le c_n\),
\[
c_n\le d_n+c_n-1<2c_n,
\]
so division by \(c_n\) has quotient \(c_{n+2}+1\). Subtracting \(1\) gives \(c_{n+2}\), as in (12).

We can now identify the original sequence with \((c_n)\). We prove by strong induction that
\[
b_n=c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{13}
\]
For \(n=0,1\), this follows from the definitions. Suppose (13) is known through indices \(k+1\). By the original recurrence (1), the induction hypothesis, and (12),
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{k+2}
&=\left\lceil\frac{b_{k+1}^2}{b_k}\right\rceil-1\\
&=\left\lceil\frac{c_{k+1}^2}{c_k}\right\rceil-1\\
&=c_{k+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (13) for all \(n\). It also retrospectively establishes that every \(b_n\) is positive, because every \(c_n\) is positive by (4), so all ratio manipulations in the original definition are legitimate.

In particular,
\[
b_2=c_2=63.
\]
For every \(k\ge0\), (3) and (13) give, as an equality of integers,
\[
b_{k+3}=4b_{k+2}-b_k. \tag{14}
\]
The right-hand side is positive because it equals \(c_{k+3}>0\); hence (14) is also the same equality if subtraction is regarded as subtraction of natural numbers. Replacing \(k+3\) by \(n\), we have proved
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}\qquad(n\ge3),
\]
together with \(b_0=4,b_1=16,b_2=63\).

It remains to translate this recurrence into the generating function. Let
\[
B(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary formal generating series. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in
\[
(1-4x+x^3)B(x)
\]
is as follows. At degree \(0\), it is \(b_0=4\). At degree \(1\), it is
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0.
\]
At degree \(2\), it is
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
For every \(n\ge3\), it is
\[
b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3}=0
\]
by (2). Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)B(x)=4-x^2.
\]
Since the denominator has constant term \(1\), it is invertible as a formal power series, and consequently
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle B(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Thus the sequence produced by the original greatest-integer consecutive-ratio rule satisfies the claimed linear recurrence and has exactly the conjectured generating function.
